newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti may sell PCs but recovery distant.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti may sell PCs but recovery distant.

text.p: Olivetti is believed to be on the verge of selling its ailing personal computer business but chief executive Roberto Colaninno still has his work cut out to turn the high-technology group around, analysts said on Wednesday.
Newspapers and analysts estimated a deal to rid the group of its PC division, widely seen as a big liability, could be worth around 200 billion lire ($130 million) in cash and debt reduction.
But the weight of high debt charges and less than glittering profitability at Olivetti's systems and services division mean Colaninno must address serious restructuring this year.

"Selling PCs is the first step, something the market was waiting for," said one Milan-based analyst. "But longer term there are still too many doubts on this company to say all the problems are over."
Olivetti shares have climbed to their highest level since early September, when the full extent of its financial problems came to light and a dramatic board room shake-up ensued.
They are now at 619 lire per share from 530 in December with traders betting a buyer has been found for the loss-making PC operations. In fact two groups are said to be in the running.

U.S. financier Edward Gottesman of the Centenary group is working on a bid with Zanussi chairman Gianmario Rossignolo while U.S. corporate debt trader Gary Klesch, head of London-based Klesch and Co, is also reported to be interested.

But no matter what the final size of a deal is, even stripping out PCs from Olivetti's current results leaves Colaninno with a company unable to cover its financial charges, said Alberto Rolla, analyst at Milan broker Pasfin.
Olivetti's net financial debt at the end of November 1996 stood at 2.916 trillion lire, compared with 3.028 trillion in October.
"Even if you strip out 800 billion for what they will get from all the restructuring they have declared, you are left with a total debt burden of about two trillion," Rolla said.
This would give annual financial charges of about 200 billion lire. "With Olivetti's new structure it's very difficult to generate an operating income of 200 billion," Rolla said.

Marie-Christine Keith, equity analyst at James Capel in London, estimated net debt at 2.35 trillion after the sale late last year to Bell Atlantic of an 8.26 percent stake in Omnitel Sistemi Radiocellulari, which owns 70 percent of Italian mobile phone service operator Omnitel Pronto Italia (OPI).

"(Sale of the PC division) leaves Olivetti looking how they want it to look -- with systems and services at the moment supplying the bulk of the sales and OPI the growing part of the business," Keith said.
But she expected further divestments would be necessary to reduce debt and make the group a leaner, meaner outfit.

A Milan analyst who declined to be named said profitability had deteriorated at the systems and services division and while the sector had reasonably good prospects in the next few years, "the problem is whether Olivetti can maintain competitiveness."
Fixed costs were too high, as were staffing levels. Clients signing new contracts needed to be sure Olivetti would still exist in a few years to fulfil those contracts, he said.
